NeurofeedbackA guided walk-through

Educational illustrations. Waveforms are simulated. Nothing here is a diagnosis or medical advice.

Overview

What neurofeedback is, and what to expect

Neurofeedback is training for the brain's own activity. Sensors read your brain's rhythms, software turns them into picture and sound, and your brain uses that information to practise steadier, more flexible patterns.

  • The sensors only listenNothing is sent into your head. The sensors read tiny electrical signals your brain already produces, the same kind a hospital EEG records.
  • It is learning, not a procedureChange comes from repetition, the way any skill does. That is why sessions are regular and why what you notice between them matters.
  • It sits alongside your other careTherapy, medication, sleep, movement and anything else that supports you are welcome at the same time. Medication decisions stay with your prescriber.

Questions this guide answers

    Research on neurofeedback is active and its results are mixed: stronger for some concerns than others, and still debated in places. The section called What research says lays that out plainly so you can decide with clear information.

    The signal

    Brain rhythms

    A sensor on the scalp picks up one tangled signal. Software separates it by speed, the way a prism separates white light into colours.

    State
    Time shown
    What one sensor records
    Every rhythm at once, added together
      About this picture. The traces are simulated and sized for the screen, and the bars show relative level only. A real recording is messier, differs from person to person, and looks different at each spot on the head. Band edges also vary a little between labs and software.
      • All of them, all the timeEvery brain produces every one of these rhythms around the clock. What changes from moment to moment is the mix.
      • Where and when matterThe same rhythm means different things at the front or the back of the head, with eyes open or closed, at rest or on a task.
      • No good or bad wavesNo rhythm is good or bad, and no pattern diagnoses a condition. What matters is flexibility: shifting gear when the moment calls for it.

      The signal

      Where the sensors go, and why stillness helps

      Sensor positions follow a worldwide map of the head. The brain's signal is tiny, so a blink or a tight jaw can drown it out.

      Show

      Seen from above, nose at the top, your left on the left. Choose any position.

      Reading the names

      Letter
      The region underneath: F frontal, C central, T temporal, P parietal, O occipital. Fp is the very front.
      Number
      Odd numbers are on the left, even numbers on the right. A z means the midline.
      Spacing
      Positions are measured as 10% and 20% steps between landmarks on your own head, so the map fits every head size. It is called the 10-20 system.

      T3, T4, T5 and T6 are written T7, T8, P7 and P8 in the newer naming.

      Brain signal, and everything else

      Try
        • The signal is tinyBrain activity at the scalp is measured in millionths of a volt. Eyes, muscles and movement produce signals many times larger.
        • Software cannot always tellLeft alone, a blink can read as slow brain activity and a tight jaw as fast activity. That would reward the wrong thing.
        • So we keep it cleanFeedback pauses during blinks and movement, I check the signal during set-up, and for a brain map the noisy stretches are removed before analysis.
        Sources and notes
        1. Marcuse, Fields & Yoo. Rowan's Primer of EEG, 2nd ed. Chapter 1: origin of the EEG signal, eye, muscle, movement and electrode artifacts.
        2. Demos. Getting Started with EEG Neurofeedback, 2nd ed. Chapter 5: the 10-20 system and brain maps.

        Region descriptions are broad associations. Every task draws on networks spanning many regions, and a sensor picks up activity from a wide area beneath it.

        What shifts your brain rhythms

        Sleep, caffeine, medication and practice all nudge the mix of rhythms. That is why I ask about them, and why a recording is read in the context of your day.

        Colour is the selected situation. Grey is rested and relaxed, for comparison.

          Typical direction of change at the group level, drawn to be visible. Real effects depend on dose, timing, tolerance and the person. A question mark means studies disagree.

          Sources and notes

            Each item was checked against published reviews or controlled studies in November 2026. Several popular claims did not hold up and are shown here as mixed or uncertain: for example that caffeine raises beta, that cannabis raises theta, that nicotine lowers alpha, or that screen use leaves a lasting brainwave pattern.

            The training

            How the training works

            Your brain's activity is measured, turned into picture and sound within a fraction of a second, and shown back to you. With that information, the brain adjusts itself.

            1. Your brainproduces its rhythms, as it always does.
            2. Sensorspick the signal up at the scalp. They only read.
            3. Amplifier and softwaremeasure the part of the signal we are training, many times a second.
            4. Picture and soundchange with that measurement: brighter, clearer, fuller.
            5. Your brain, againtakes in the change and adjusts, mostly without effort. Then the loop repeats.
            Kind of feedback
            what you watch
            The picture stands in for the film, game or sounds used in a real session.
            • It is not a testThere is nothing to get right. Trying hard tends to get in the way. Comfortable, curious attention is all that is asked.
            • Feedback only ever rewardsWhen the signal drifts, the picture and sound simply ease off. Nothing is punished and nothing is pushed into the brain.
            • Repetition does the workOne session is practice. Change builds across many sessions, which is why regular attendance matters.
            Sources and notes
            1. Sitaram et al. Closed-loop brain training: the science of neurofeedback. Nat Rev Neurosci, 2017. link
            2. Dessy et al. Train your brain? Can we really selectively train specific EEG frequencies with neurofeedback training. Front Hum Neurosci, 2020. link
            3. Maaz et al. Non-specific increase in alpha power during a neurofeedback session targeting its downregulation. Imaging Neurosci, 2026 (within one session, alpha rose in every group, including sham). link
            4. Weber et al. Predictors of neurofeedback training outcome: a systematic review. NeuroImage Clin, 2020. link
            5. Demos. Getting Started with EEG Neurofeedback, 2nd ed., chapters 1 and 6 (reward and inhibit thresholds). Collura. Technical Foundations of Neurofeedback, chapter 1.
            6. Kirk (ed.). Restoring the Brain, 2nd ed., chapters 2 and 3 (infra-low frequency training described by its developers as continuous feedback without thresholds).
            7. Othmer & Othmer. Endogenous neuromodulation at infra-low frequency: method and theory. Preprint, 2024 (training without overt reinforcement, at a frequency specific to each person). link

            The standard scientific account is learning inside a closed loop. Studies show many people can learn to change a trained rhythm, though not everyone does, and how specific the change is to the trained rhythm is still debated. The signal on this page is simulated.

            The training

            Kinds of training

            The approaches I use differ mainly in how fast or slow the rhythms are that they work with, and in whether you are reaching a target or simply being shown your own signal.

            Approach

            Each step to the right is ten times faster. The left end is one wave in nearly three hours; the right end is a hundred waves a second.

            How they fit together. We begin with what suits your goals and how settled your system is, usually the steadier foundation work first. Other approaches are added only if and when they fit. Not everyone uses all of them.
            How I choose. From our assessment interview, from a brain map if you have one, and above all from how you respond. Your reports during and between sessions guide every adjustment.
            Sources and notes
            1. Kirk (ed.). Restoring the Brain, 2nd ed., chapters 2 and 3: infra-low frequency training, its frequency range, and tuning to the individual's response.

            4. Demos. Getting Started with EEG Neurofeedback, 2nd ed., chapters 5 and 6: brain maps; reward and inhibit training.
            5. Bazzana et al. Infra-low frequency neurofeedback: a systematic mixed studies review. Front Hum Neurosci, 2022. link
            6. Othmer & Othmer. Endogenous neuromodulation at infra-low frequency: method and theory. Preprint, 2024 (training without overt reinforcement, at a frequency specific to each person). link

            The training

            What your sessions will be like

            Each visit is about an hour, with 30 to 45 minutes of actual training. Two or three visits a week works best when your schedule allows.

            The hour

            Check-inSet-upTraining · 30 to 45 minutesWrap-up
            1. Check-inHow you have been since last time: sleep, mood, energy, focus, anything new. We update your symptom tracking.
            2. Set-upSensors go on with a little paste. I check the signal and sort out any trouble spots before we start.
            3. TrainingYou sit comfortably and watch and listen while the feedback runs. I stay with you, watch the signal, and adjust as needed.
            4. Wrap-upSensors off and clean-up, how the session felt, anything to look out for, and scheduling.

            From first meeting onward

            1. Assessment interviewYour history, current concerns, sleep, health, medications, and what you hope will change.
            2. Brain map, if it fitsOffered when it is appropriate and you want one. Some people are not ready for one yet or prefer not to have one, and we can plan without it.
            3. Regular trainingAbout an hour a visit, ideally two or three times a week, with your reports steering each session.
            4. Review as we goWe look at your tracking together at regular points and decide whether to continue, change approach, space sessions out, or stop.

            Planning a block

            Sessions
            A week

            For planning only. Studies have typically used about 15 to 40 sessions. Your number depends on your goals and how you respond, and we review it together as we go.

            Evidence on spacing is limited. One trial in athletes, and a pooled analysis of ADHD studies, favoured three sessions a week over fewer.

            What you might notice

            Most reactions are mild and pass within a day: feeling tired, wired, headachy, spacey or more emotional than usual, or a change in sleep or dreams. More vivid dreams are one that clients often mention, though that comes from clinical observation and has not been tested in trials. Some people notice nothing at first.

            In large trials no serious harm from training has been reported, and passing reactions like these are common even in comparison groups given sham feedback. Where trials tracked them closely, they were most common in the first two weeks.

            Tell me about all of it, pleasant or not. A reaction is information. It tells me how to adjust the training, and the adjustment usually settles it.

            Your part

            • Notice and report. What changes during and between sessions, for better or worse, is the main thing that guides the training.
            • Keep taking medication as prescribed. Any change is for you and your prescriber to decide. Please tell me when one happens, so I can read your responses correctly.
            • Keep up everything else that helps. Therapy, exercise, sleep routines and other treatments are all welcome alongside this.
            • Come as you are. If you slept badly or the day has been hard, say so. It shapes the session and nothing is wasted.
            Sources and notes

            3. Schönenberg et al. Neurofeedback, sham neurofeedback, and cognitive-behavioural group therapy in adults with ADHD: a triple-blind, randomised, controlled trial. Lancet Psychiatry, 2017. link
            4. Domingos et al. Session frequency matters in neurofeedback training of athletes. Appl Psychophysiol Biofeedback, 2021. link

            The evidence

            What the research says

            A plain summary of where neurofeedback research stands, including what is still unsettled. Reviewed against published studies in November 2026.

            • Most people who train improveAcross trials, people who complete neurofeedback usually report meaningful improvement, often large. Where studies followed people up, the gains generally held.
            • Why they improve is debatedIn the most rigorous trials, people given sham feedback often improve about as much. Part of the benefit may come from the whole experience: regular sessions, focused practice, support and expectation.
            • It appears safeLarge trials report no serious harm from training. Reactions are usually mild and short-lived.
            Show
            Well supported Promising, debated Emerging Early

            The levels are a reading of the published evidence for adults, not a prediction for any one person. Choose a row for the detail and the studies.

            Where the research is heading

            • Larger, better-controlled trials, reported to an agreed checklist so that studies can be compared.
            • Rethinking comparison conditions. Sham feedback turns out to be partly active, which makes "real versus sham" harder to interpret than it sounds.
            • Working out who learns and who benefits. Many participants do not show the trained change, and early learning seems to predict the rest.
            • More personalised protocols, guided by a person's own rhythms or brain map.
            • Brain-imaging studies of what changes with training, and well-tested home devices.

            What this means for us

            I offer neurofeedback as one part of your care, alongside whatever else is helping you, and not in place of treatments with stronger evidence.

            We track your own response from the start: your goals, your symptom ratings and what you notice. If training is helping, we will see it. If it is not, we will see that too and change course.

            All sources

              Sources were gathered with Consensus and checked against each paper's abstract. Effect sizes are group averages from the cited analyses. An SMD or g near 0.2 is conventionally small, 0.5 moderate and 0.8 large.

              The body

              Heart and breath

              Your heart does not tick like a clock. It speeds up a little as you breathe in and slows as you breathe out. Slow, gentle breathing makes that swing larger, and practising it is called heart-rate variability biofeedback.

              Signal
              --beats a minute
              Swing with the breath
              -- beats a minute
              Beat-to-beat variation (RMSSD, last minute)
              -- ms

              Heart rate, beat by beat, over the last minute. Shaded stretches are in-breaths on the pacer. Look for a smooth wave that rises with each in-breath and falls with each out-breath.

              Breaths a minute
              Rhythm

              Finding your pace

              Most adults get their largest swing somewhere between 4.5 and 6.5 breaths a minute. Stay at each pace for a minute or two and compare. Each pace you try is logged here.

              Breaths a minuteBreaths countedAverage swing
              Near enough is good enough: in a four-week trial, training at a personal pace and at a fixed 6 a minute worked about equally well.
              Breathe gently. Slower, not bigger. If you feel light-headed, tingly or short of air, you are over-breathing: take smaller, softer breaths, or go back to breathing normally.
              A small swing is not a bad sign. The swing naturally gets smaller with age and varies with fitness and some medications. In one study, healthy but inactive men in their sixties swung about 10 beats a minute during slow breathing, compared with about 22 in young men. What matters is how your own pattern changes with practice.
              What practice does. Across 58 randomized trials, this kind of training showed small-to-moderate benefits, largest for anxiety, low mood, anger and performance. Programmes usually ask for short daily practice, often under 20 minutes. Benefits are clearer in people with symptoms than in healthy people, and not everyone responds in the same way.

              For learning only. This is not a medical device and cannot detect heart problems. If your rhythm looks irregular, or you have a heart or breathing condition, talk with your physician before practising.
